## 10. Future work

The theorem converts the open question from "which divisibility feature is it?" into "which aperiodic feature is it?", and supplies a quantitative screen for candidates.

**1. An aperiodic-carrier classification theorem.** "Position dial" now has an exact meaning: non-invariance of window composition under translation. For finite-valued classifiers, translation invariance of composition at all window lengths is essentially equivalent to periodicity, and Theorem 6.3 supplies the exact drift bound $L \bmod m$ that any classification theorem must beat. The natural target: a finite-valued classifier whose window composition drifts by more than $C/L$ is not almost periodic, and its Fourier–Bohr spectrum must contain an irrational frequency. This would replace the modulus-by-modulus screen with a single spectral criterion.

**2. Size and valuation carriers — the surviving candidates.** The classifiers that Theorem 6.6 does *not* kill are those that see magnitude rather than residue: the actual size of $v = j^2 - N$ as $j$ traverses the window (which grows monotonically and hence aperiodically), proximity to a truncation or logarithm-threshold boundary in the sieve, and $p$-adic valuations of $v$ beyond mere divisibility — $v_p(v) \ge 2$ events are rarer and interact with the size gradient. These are the natural next tests, and each can be pre-screened by Algorithm C before any expensive run.

**3. Transfer across bit lengths.** Because the drift budget $\delta \ge (\rho-1)/(\rho+1)$ is scale-free, the same test applies verbatim at any modulus size. A worthwhile experiment is to measure $\rho$ as a function of bit length: if the excess amplitude is stable, the required drift budget is stable too, and a single carrier of fixed relative width is implicated.

**4. Sharpening the estimator null.** The disclosed gap between the raw $z = 4.11$ and the null-calibrated $z_{\mathrm{cal}} = 1.53$ is a statement about max-over-bins bias, not about the effect. A shape-matched test statistic — projecting the residual onto a fixed bump template rather than taking a maximum — would remove the selection bias by construction and give a calibrated significance directly comparable to the structural bound of Theorem 5.4.

---

## 11. Conclusion

A four-sigma mid-window excess in a smooth-value hit profile survived a sixteen-cell divisibility mixture baseline with exactly $0\%$ removal and an unmoved peak. We showed this is not an empirical accident but a theorem. The divisibility cell of $j^2-N$ is $210$-periodic in $j$, so window composition is exactly position-independent; under flat composition the whole mixture family collapses to the one-dimensional ray $\{K\cdot B\}$, and every ratio-based excess statistic, together with its argmax, is invariant under the fit. The robust version gives a scale-free drift budget: absorbing a relative excess $\rho-1$ requires composition drift at least $(\rho-1)/(\rho+1)$, i.e. $8.1\%$ here against a measured $0.269\%$. Because only periodicity was used, the result extends to every classifier factoring through $\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z}$ — power residues, Legendre symbols, bit patterns — and the mechanism behind the excess is therefore constrained to be aperiodic in $j$. Sharpness results confirm that positional families do remove $100\%$ of the same excess and that aperiodic carriers with position-dependent composition exist, so the negative result is about the arithmetic grid and not about the method.

\begin{abstract}
Sieve-based factoring methods scan the polynomial values $v = j^2 - N$ and record
which of them are smooth. A measured mid-window excess in the smooth-hit
profile --- a residual peak of relative amplitude $0.1774 \pm 0.0432$ at
normalized window coordinate $t = 0.65$, against a Dickman-weighted reference
--- was tested against a sixteen-cell divisibility mixture baseline, in which
candidates are stratified by the pattern $(2 \mid v,\, 3\mid v,\, 5\mid v,\, 7
\mid v)$ and each cell is granted its own free rate. The mixture removed exactly
$0\%$ of the excess and left the peak position unmoved.

We prove that this outcome is forced. The cell label of $j^2 - N$ is a
$210$-periodic function of $j$, so every window of $210$ consecutive candidates
has \emph{identical} cell populations regardless of position; we call this
\emph{flat composition}. Under flat composition the entire $|C|$-parameter
mixture family collapses to the ray $\{K\cdot B\}$ spanned by a single common
shape $B$: the model has one degree of freedom, a rate, and none in position.
Consequently the residual relative excess and its argmax are exact invariants of
the fit, and removal is identically zero. We give the robust quantitative form:
with per-cell relative drift $\delta$, the excess ratio $\rho$ can shrink by at
most the factor $(1-\delta)/(1+\delta)$; inverting, absorbing a relative excess
$\rho-1$ requires $\delta \ge (\rho-1)/(\rho+1)$, i.e.\ $8.1\%$ here against a
measured $0.269\%$. Finally we remove an entire family of candidate mechanisms:
\emph{any} classifier of $j$ factoring through $\Z/m\Z$ --- higher power
residues, Legendre symbols at primes $p>7$, bit patterns, Boolean combinations
--- has flat composition on windows of length a multiple of $m$ and removes
$0\%$. The carrier of the observed positional excess must be aperiodic in $j$.
Two sharpness results confirm the hypothesis is not vacuous.
\end{abstract}

\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} smooth values, Dickman function, quadratic sieve,
mixture baseline, periodic classifier, window composition, positional excess,
rate modulation.

\section{Introduction}

\subsection{The setting}
Congruence-of-squares factoring methods generate candidate values along a
polynomial sequence and retain those that are \emph{smooth} --- completely
factorable over a fixed prime base. For the classical quadratic-sieve polynomial
the sequence is
\[
v(j) \;=\; j^2 - N, \qquad j = j_0, j_0+1, \dots, j_0 + L - 1,
\]
with $j_0 \approx \lceil \sqrt N \rceil$ and $L$ the scan-window length. The
expected \emph{rate} of smooth hits is classically modelled by the Dickman
function $\rho$: the density of $y$-smooth integers near $x$ is $\approx\rho(u)$
with $u = \log x/\log y$. Writing $t\in[0,1]$ for the normalized position within
the window, the Dickman-weighted reference profile $B(t)$ is a smooth,
featureless, gently varying curve.

\subsection{The observation}
Empirically the ratio of measured to predicted hits, $R(t) = T(t)/B(t)$, is
\emph{not} featureless: it carries a reproducible interior peak. At $t = 0.65$
the residual exceeds the flank level by a relative amplitude
\[
\mathrm{amp} \;=\; 0.1774 \pm 0.0432, \qquad z = 4.11,
\]
above the pre-registered detection bar $z \ge 2$. The feature is stable under
translation of the window and reappears across choices of $N$. Prior stages
established that the feature is real over an exact Dickman baseline and that no
single binary divisibility indicator explains it. The remaining natural
hypothesis is a \emph{composition} effect: if the mixture of candidate types
drifted with $t$, an apparent positional excess would arise with no positional
mechanism behind it.

\subsection{The mixture baseline and its failure}
Stratify candidates by their small-prime divisibility pattern
\[
c(j) \;=\; \bigl(2\mid v(j),\ 3\mid v(j),\ 5\mid v(j),\ 7\mid v(j)\bigr)\in\{0,1\}^4,
\]
giving $|C| = 16$ cells; compute per-cell Dickman-weighted reference sums
$S_c(t)$ and fit per-cell rates $\kappa_c$ on the window flanks, with the score
region excluded and shrinkage toward the global flank rate. The corrected
baseline is $\PRED(t) = \sum_c \kappa_c S_c(t)$. The fitted rates were genuinely
modulated --- normalized rates spread over $[0.645, 1.406]$, a factor $\approx
2.2$, the largest cells being combinations involving $3\mid v$ and $5\mid v$ ---
yet the residual peak was untouched: amplitude $0.1774$, peak at $t = 0.65$,
removal $0\%$. Separately, class composition was measured flat in $t$ to a
maximum cell drift of $0.269\%$. This paper explains, and proves, why.

\subsection{Contributions}
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{Structure} (\S\ref{sec:part1}). The divisibility cell of $j^2-N$ is
$210$-periodic in $j$; every window of $210$ consecutive $j$ has identical cell
populations, for every $N$ and every position. For odd $N$, the bit $2\mid v$ is
exactly the parity of $j$.
\item \textbf{Collapse} (\S\ref{sec:part2}). Flat composition forces
$\sum_c\kappa_cS_c = K\cdot B$; the achievable prediction set is exactly the ray
$\{K\cdot B\}$. Hence residual invariance, exact $0\%$ removal, argmax
invariance, non-fittability.
\item \textbf{Robustness} (\S\ref{sec:part3}). With drift $\delta$ the excess
ratio shrinks by at most $(1-\delta)/(1+\delta)$; inverting gives a scale-free
drift budget.
\item \textbf{Family removal} (\S\ref{sec:part4}). Every $\Z/m\Z$-factoring
classifier is $m$-periodic, hence flat, hence removes $0\%$. The carrier must be
aperiodic.
\item \textbf{Sharpness} (\S\ref{sec:part5}). A positional family removes $100\%$
of the same excess; an explicit aperiodic carrier with position-dependent
composition exists.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Definitions}
Throughout, $N\in\Z$, $j$ ranges over $\Z$, and $v(j) = j^2 - N$. Let $C$ be a
finite set of \emph{cells}.

\begin{definition}[Divisibility cell]
For $v\in\Z$ set
$\cellOf(v) = \bigl([2\mid v],[3\mid v],[5\mid v],[7\mid v]\bigr)\in\{0,1\}^4$,
and $\cellN(j) = \cellOf(j^2-N)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Window count]
For a classifier $f:\Z\to C$, a start $a\in\Z$, a length $L\in\Nat$ and a class
$c$,
\[
\cnt_f(a,L,c) \;=\; \#\{\, i\in\{0,\dots,L-1\} : f(a+i) = c \,\}.
\]
For the divisibility grid at length $210$ we write
$\wcount_N(a,c) = \cnt_{\cellN}(a,210,c)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Periodic classifier]
$f:\Z\to C$ is \emph{$m$-periodic} if $f(j+m) = f(j)$ for all $j$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Flat composition]\label{def:flat}
A cell-resolved reference family $S:C\times\R\to\R$ has \emph{flat composition}
with weights $w:C\to\R$ and common shape $B:\R\to\R$ if
\[
S_c(t) \;=\; w_c\cdot B(t) \qquad\text{for all } c\in C,\ t\in\R.
\]
Every cell contributes a fixed \emph{fraction} of one and the same positional
shape; the cell decomposition carries no information about $t$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Mixture prediction]
For rates $\kappa: C\to\R$, \ $\PRED_\kappa(t) = \sum_{c\in C}\kappa_c S_c(t)$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Residual and relative excess]
For a measured profile $T$ and baseline $P$,
\[
\Res[T,P](t) = \frac{T(t)}{P(t)},\qquad
\Exc[R](t_0,t_1) = \frac{R(t_0)}{R(t_1)} - 1 .
\]
Here $t_0 = 0.65$ is the peak and $t_1$ a flank reference. The \emph{removal
fraction} is the difference between the excess computed against the fitted
mixture and the one computed against $B$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Cell reference sums]\label{def:cellref}
The experiment's per-cell references are window populations weighted by the
common Dickman shape: $S_c(t) = \wcount_N(\lfloor t\rfloor, c)\cdot B(t)$.
\end{definition}

\section{Part I --- The divisibility grid is \texorpdfstring{$210$}{210}-periodic
and its composition is flat}\label{sec:part1}

\begin{lemma}[Cell labels see only $v \bmod 210$]\label{lem:cellmod}
For all $v,k\in\Z$, $\cellOf(v+210k) = \cellOf(v)$.
\end{lemma}
\begin{proof}
$210 = 2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7$, so for each $p\in\{2,3,5,7\}$ we have $p\mid 210k$,
whence $p\mid v+210k \iff p\mid v$. All four coordinates of the label agree.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Periodicity of the sieve cell]\label{thm:cellper}
For every $N$ and $j$, \ $\cellN(j+210) = \cellN(j)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
$(j+210)^2 - N = (j^2-N) + 210(2j+210)$; apply Lemma~\ref{lem:cellmod} with
$k = 2j+210$.
\end{proof}

No hypothesis on $N$ is required: the statement holds for every integer $N$,
whatever its factorization.

\begin{theorem}[Shift invariance of window populations]\label{thm:shift}
For every $N$, $a$, $c$, \ $\wcount_N(a+1,c) = \wcount_N(a,c)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Write $h(i) = [\cellN(a+i) = c]$. Summing $h$ over $\{0,\dots,210\}$ in the two
standard ways gives
$\sum_{i=0}^{209}h(i+1) + h(0) = \sum_{i=0}^{209}h(i) + h(210)$.
By Theorem~\ref{thm:cellper}, $\cellN(a+210) = \cellN(a)$, so $h(210) = h(0)$ and
the two remaining sums coincide; they are $\wcount_N(a+1,c)$ and
$\wcount_N(a,c)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Flat composition of the divisibility grid]\label{cor:flatgrid}
For all $N,a,b,c$, \ $\wcount_N(a,c) = \wcount_N(b,c) = \wcount_N(0,c)$.
\end{corollary}
\begin{proof}
Induct on $a$ in both directions from $0$ using Theorem~\ref{thm:shift}.
\end{proof}

Equivalently, in the language of Definition~\ref{def:flat}: with
$w_c = \wcount_N(0,c)$ the family of Definition~\ref{def:cellref} has flat
composition. This is the exact structural counterpart of the measured statement
``class composition flat in $t$, maximum cell drift $0.269\%$''.

\subsection{Parity lives inside the grid}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:parity}
Let $N$ be odd. Then $2\mid j^2-N \iff j$ is odd.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Write $N = 2m+1$. If $j = 2k+1$ then $j^2-N = 2(2k^2+2k-m)$ is even; if $j = 2k$
then $j^2-N = 2(2k^2-m)-1$ is odd.
\end{proof}

Bit $0$ of the grid is precisely $j$-parity, so any residual ``parity carrier''
reading is already inside the sixteen-cell model and fails with it.

\subsection{The rates are real: quadratic-residue modulation}
Flatness in position is not flatness in rate. For an odd prime $p$,
\[
\#\{\, j\in\Z/p : j^2 = N \,\} \;=\; 1 + \left(\tfrac{N}{p}\right)\in\{0,1,2\},
\]
so the rate at which $p$ divides $v$ is $0$, $1/p$ or $2/p$ according as $N$ is a
non-residue, zero, or a residue mod $p$. At $p = 3$ the count is $1$ if
$N\equiv0$, $2$ if $N\equiv1$, $0$ if $N\equiv2$; at $p = 7$, $N\equiv3$ gives
$0$ roots and $N\equiv1$ gives $2$.

\paragraph{Worked table ($N = 8051 = 83\cdot97$).}
$8051$ is odd and $8051\equiv 2 \pmod 3$, a non-residue. Every window of $210$
consecutive $j$ contains exactly:

\begin{center}
\begin{tabular}{lc}
\toprule
cell $(2\mid v,3\mid v,5\mid v,7\mid v)$ & population\\
\midrule
$(0,0,0,0)$ & $45$\\
$(0,0,0,1)$ & $18$\\
$(0,0,1,0)$ & $30$\\
$(0,0,1,1)$ & $12$\\
$(1,0,0,0)$ & $45$\\
$(1,0,0,1)$ & $18$\\
$(1,0,1,0)$ & $30$\\
$(1,0,1,1)$ & $12$\\
any cell with $3\mid v$ & $0$\\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{center}

The parity bit splits the window exactly in half, $45+18+30+12 = 105$ odd $j$ and
$105$ even $j$, as Proposition~\ref{prop:parity} requires; all eight $3\mid v$
cells are empty by the non-residue condition. By
Corollary~\ref{cor:flatgrid} these same populations occur at \emph{every} window
start. The dial is genuinely turned --- a cell rate of exactly $0$ is as
modulated as a rate gets --- and it never turns with position.

\section{Part II --- Flat composition collapses the mixture to a
ray}\label{sec:part2}

Fix a finite cell set $C$, a family $S$ with flat composition $S_c = w_cB$, and
write $K(\kappa) = \sum_c \kappa_c w_c$.

\begin{theorem}[Collapse]\label{thm:collapse}
For all $\kappa$ and $t$, \ $\PRED_\kappa(t) = K(\kappa)\cdot B(t)$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
$\sum_c\kappa_cS_c(t) = \sum_c\kappa_cw_cB(t) = \bigl(\sum_c\kappa_cw_c\bigr)B(t)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The mixture family is exactly a ray]
If $w_{c_0}\ne0$ for some $c_0$, then
$\{\PRED_\kappa : \kappa\in\R^C\} = \{K\cdot B : K\in\R\}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Inclusion $\subseteq$ is Theorem~\ref{thm:collapse}. For $\supseteq$, given $K$
take $\kappa_{c_0} = K/w_{c_0}$ and $\kappa_c = 0$ otherwise; then
$K(\kappa) = K$.
\end{proof}

Thus the $|C|$-parameter model has exactly one effective parameter, and it is a
scale. No choice of rates changes the shape.

\begin{corollary}[No positional freedom]
For all $\kappa,\kappa'$ and all $s,t$,
$\PRED_\kappa(t)\PRED_{\kappa'}(s) = \PRED_\kappa(s)\PRED_{\kappa'}(t)$: any two
mixtures are pointwise proportional.
\end{corollary}

\begin{lemma}[Residual rescaling]\label{lem:rescale}
$\Res[T,\PRED_\kappa](t) = \Res[T,B](t)/K(\kappa)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Invariance of the amplitude; removal is exactly $0\%$]
\label{thm:invariance}
Let $K(\kappa)\ne0$, $T(t_1)\ne0$, $B(t_1)\ne0$. Then
\[
\Exc\bigl[\Res[T,\PRED_\kappa]\bigr](t_0,t_1)
\;=\;\Exc\bigl[\Res[T,B]\bigr](t_0,t_1),
\]
and hence the removal fraction, the difference of the two, is identically $0$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By Lemma~\ref{lem:rescale} both residuals differ by the constant factor
$1/K(\kappa)$, which cancels in the ratio $R(t_0)/R(t_1)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The peak does not move]\label{thm:peak}
If $K(\kappa) > 0$ and $t_0$ maximizes $\Res[T,B]$ over a set $W$, then $t_0$
maximizes $\Res[T,\PRED_\kappa]$ over $W$; strict maxima remain strict.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Dividing by the positive constant $K(\kappa)$ preserves $\le$ and $<$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Non-fittability]
If $T(t_0)B(t_1)\ne T(t_1)B(t_0)$, then $\PRED_\kappa\ne T$ for every $\kappa$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
$\PRED_\kappa = T$ would give $T(t_i) = K(\kappa)B(t_i)$ for $i = 0,1$, forcing
proportionality.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Capstone for the divisibility grid]
For every $N$, every shape $B$, every measured profile $T$, and every
$\kappa\in\R^{16}$ with $\sum_c\kappa_c\wcount_N(0,c)\ne0$,
\[
\Exc\bigl[\Res[T,\textstyle\sum_c\kappa_cS_c]\bigr](t_0,t_1)
= \Exc\bigl[\Res[T,B]\bigr](t_0,t_1),
\]
with $S_c$ as in Definition~\ref{def:cellref}. Contrapositively, a nonzero
mid-window excess over the plain shape forces a nonzero excess over
\emph{every} divisibility mixture.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Corollary~\ref{cor:flatgrid} gives flat composition with
$w_c = \wcount_N(0,c)$; apply Theorem~\ref{thm:invariance}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}[Slogan]
\emph{Divisibility is a rate dial, not a position dial.} The sixteen cells buy a
global scale factor; the sought mechanism lives in $t$, where the model has no
reach at all.
\end{remark}

\section{Part III --- Robust form: drift budgets}\label{sec:part3}

Real windows are finite and real compositions are flat only to measurement
precision (here $0.269\%$).

\begin{definition}[Relative composition drift]
$S$ has drift at most $\delta\ge0$ at $t$ (relative to $w$ and $B$) if
$\bigl|S_c(t) - w_cB(t)\bigr| \le \delta\,\bigl(w_cB(t)\bigr)$ for every $c$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Squeeze]
If $\kappa_c\ge0$ for all $c$ and $S$ has drift at most $\delta$ at $t$, then
\[
(1-\delta)K(\kappa)B(t) \;\le\; \PRED_\kappa(t) \;\le\; (1+\delta)K(\kappa)B(t).
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Bound each $S_c(t)$ between $(1\pm\delta)w_cB(t)$, multiply by $\kappa_c\ge0$ and
sum.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Excess lower bound]\label{thm:excbound}
Let $B(t_0),B(t_1)>0$, $T(t_0)\ge0$, $T(t_1)>0$, and let $P(t_0),P(t_1)>0$ satisfy
\[
P(t_0)\le(1+\delta)KB(t_0),\qquad P(t_1)\ge(1-\delta)KB(t_1),
\]
with $0\le\delta<1$. If $T(t_0)B(t_1) = \rho\,T(t_1)B(t_0)$, then
\[
\frac{T(t_0)/P(t_0)}{T(t_1)/P(t_1)} \;\ge\; \rho\cdot\frac{1-\delta}{1+\delta}.
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Substitute the two one-sided bounds into the cross-multiplied inequality
$\rho(1-\delta)T(t_1)P(t_0)\le(1+\delta)T(t_0)P(t_1)$: the left side is bounded
using $P(t_0)\le(1+\delta)KB(t_0)$, the right using
$P(t_1)\ge(1-\delta)KB(t_1)$, and the two meet exactly through the defining
relation $\rho\,T(t_1)B(t_0) = T(t_0)B(t_1)$. Dividing by the positive quantity
$T(t_1)P(t_0)$ gives the stated form.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Registered verdict at the measured numbers]
With $\delta = 0.00269$ and $\rho = 1.1774$, under the hypotheses of
Theorem~\ref{thm:excbound},
\[
\frac{T(t_0)/P(t_0)}{T(t_1)/P(t_1)} - 1 \;\ge\; 0.1710 .
\]
In particular the surviving excess exceeds the registered bar
$2\,\mathrm{SE} = 2\times0.0432 = 0.0864$ and also twice the null-calibrated
standard error $2\times0.0411 = 0.0822$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
$1.1774\times\frac{1-0.00269}{1+0.00269} = 1.17108\ldots \ge 1.1710$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Drift budget --- inverse form]\label{thm:budget}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:excbound}, if the mixture absorbs the
excess completely, i.e.\ $\dfrac{T(t_0)/P(t_0)}{T(t_1)/P(t_1)}\le1$, then
$\delta \ge \dfrac{\rho-1}{\rho+1}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{thm:excbound} gives $\rho(1-\delta)/(1+\delta)\le1$, i.e.\
$\rho(1-\delta)\le1+\delta$, i.e.\ $\rho-1\le\delta(\rho+1)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Measured budget]
For $\rho-1 = 0.1774$ absorption requires $\delta \ge 0.081$, i.e.\ $8.1\%$
composition drift --- more than $30\times$ the measured $0.269\%$.
\end{corollary}

Theorem~\ref{thm:budget} is the most portable statement here: it mentions no bit
length, window length, prime bound or data geometry, so the test transfers to any
problem size unchanged.

\section{Part IV --- The whole residue family is removed}\label{sec:part4}

The argument of \S\S\ref{sec:part1}--\ref{sec:part2} used exactly one property of
the divisibility grid: periodicity.

\begin{lemma}[Window calculus]\label{lem:calc}
$\cnt_f(a,L,c)\le L$, and windows concatenate:
$\cnt_f(a,L_1+L_2,c) = \cnt_f(a,L_1,c) + \cnt_f(a+L_1,L_2,c)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Flat composition for periodic classifiers]\label{thm:perflat}
If $f$ is $m$-periodic and $L = mq$ for some $q\in\Nat$, then
$\cnt_f(a,L,c) = \cnt_f(0,L,c)$ for every $a$ and $c$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
First $\cnt_f(a+1,L,c) = \cnt_f(a,L,c)$ by the telescoping identity of
Theorem~\ref{thm:shift}, whose only input is $f(a+L) = f(a)$ --- which holds
since $m\mid L$ and $f$ is $m$-periodic (iterate $f(j+m) = f(j)$ $q$ times).
Then induct on $a$ in both directions.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Bounded drift for incommensurate windows]\label{thm:drift}
If $f$ is $m$-periodic then for all $a,b,L,c$,
\[
\cnt_f(a,L,c)\;\le\;\cnt_f(b,L,c) + (L \bmod m).
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Write $L = mq+r$ with $r = L\bmod m$. Splitting the window
(Lemma~\ref{lem:calc}) gives
$\cnt_f(a,L,c) = q\,\cnt_f(0,m,c) + \cnt_f(a+mq,r,c)$, and likewise for $b$; the
$q$-terms are identical and the remainders are each at most $r$.
\end{proof}

Thus the relative composition drift of an $m$-periodic carrier over a window of
length $L$ is below $m/L$. Combined with the measured budget, an $m$-periodic
carrier can absorb the excess only if $m/L \ge 0.081$: its period must be at
least $8.1\%$ of the entire scan window.

\begin{theorem}[Every residue-type carrier is periodic]\label{thm:resper}
Let $g:\Z/m\Z\to C$ be arbitrary.
\begin{enumerate}
\item $j\mapsto g(j\bmod m)$ is $m$-periodic.
\item $j\mapsto g\bigl((j^2-N)\bmod m\bigr)$ is $m$-periodic.
\item In particular, for a prime $p$ the quadratic-character carrier
$j\mapsto\chi_p(j^2-N)$ --- the Legendre symbol $\left(\frac{j^2-N}{p}\right)$,
including the value $0$ --- is $p$-periodic.
\end{enumerate}
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
(1) $j+m\equiv j \pmod m$. (2) $(j+m)^2 - N \equiv j^2-N \pmod m$. (3) is (2)
with $g = \chi_p$.
\end{proof}

These cover the entire pre-named candidate family: divisibility patterns at any
prime set, higher power residues of $v$, Legendre and higher-character symbols
at primes $p>7$, low bit patterns of $j$ or of $v$ (functions of $v \bmod 2^k$),
and every Boolean combination thereof --- a Boolean combination of
$m_i$-periodic classifiers is $\operatorname{lcm}(m_i)$-periodic.

\begin{theorem}[Capstone: no residue mixture removes any part of the excess]
\label{thm:rescap}
Let $f$ be $m$-periodic, $L = mq$, and set
$S_c(t) = \cnt_f(\lfloor t\rfloor,L,c)\cdot B(t)$. Then for every $\kappa$ with
$\sum_c\kappa_c\cnt_f(0,L,c)\ne0$,
\[
\Exc\bigl[\Res[T,\PRED_\kappa]\bigr](t_0,t_1) = \Exc\bigl[\Res[T,B]\bigr](t_0,t_1).
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Theorem~\ref{thm:perflat} gives flat composition with $w_c = \cnt_f(0,L,c)$;
apply Theorem~\ref{thm:invariance}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The carrier must be aperiodic]
Suppose some class mixture built from a classifier $f$ on windows of length $L$
\emph{does} move the measured relative excess, i.e.
$\Exc[\Res[T,\PRED_\kappa]](t_0,t_1) \ne \Exc[\Res[T,B]](t_0,t_1)$. Then there is
no $m\mid L$ for which $f$ is $m$-periodic.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Contrapositive of Theorem~\ref{thm:rescap}.
\end{proof}

Any proposed carrier that factors through a residue system, at any modulus
commensurate with the window, is dead before it is tested.

\section{Part V --- Sharpness: the hypothesis is not vacuous}\label{sec:part5}

\begin{definition}[Positional reference family]\label{def:posfam}
Given a shape $B$ and the measurement $T$, define a two-cell family
$S^{\mathrm{pos}}_{\mathrm{false}}(t) = B(t)$,
$S^{\mathrm{pos}}_{\mathrm{true}}(t) = T(t)$. Its cells drift with $t$ whenever
$T$ is not proportional to $B$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Sharpness I: $100\%$ removal is achievable]
With $\kappa_{\mathrm{true}} = 1$, $\kappa_{\mathrm{false}} = 0$ and
$T(t_0),T(t_1)\ne0$, \ $\Exc[\Res[T,\PRED_\kappa]](t_0,t_1) = 0$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
$\PRED_\kappa = T$, so the residual is identically $1$ and its ratio across
positions is $1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}
If $T(t_0)B(t_1)\ne T(t_1)B(t_0)$, the positional family admits no weights $w$
making it flat.
\end{proposition}
\begin{proof}
Flatness would give $T(t_i) = w_{\mathrm{true}}B(t_i)$ for $i = 0,1$,
contradicting non-proportionality.
\end{proof}

So the same fitting procedure that removes $0\%$ over a periodic grid removes
$100\%$ over a positional family: the $0\%$ is a fact about the grid, not about
mixtures.

\begin{definition}[Step carrier]
$\sigma(j) = [\,j\ge0\,]\in\{0,1\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Sharpness II: aperiodic carriers with positional composition
exist]
For every $L\ge1$, \ $\cnt_\sigma(0,L,1) = L$ and $\cnt_\sigma(-L,L,1) = 0$, so
$\sigma$ has maximal composition drift; consequently $\sigma$ is not
$m$-periodic for any $m\ge1$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
The two counts are immediate. If $\sigma$ were $m$-periodic,
Theorem~\ref{thm:perflat} with $L = m$ would force the two counts to be equal,
contradicting $m\ne0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Rate-dial dichotomy]
Let $S$ have flat composition with shape $B$, and let $T(t_0),T(t_1)\ne0$,
$B(t_1)\ne0$. Then simultaneously: (i) for \emph{every} $\kappa$ with
$K(\kappa)\ne0$ the mixture over $S$ preserves the relative excess exactly; and
(ii) the positional family of Definition~\ref{def:posfam} annihilates the same
excess.
\end{theorem}

Divisibility --- and every residue classification --- is a rate dial; whatever
carries the $t\approx0.65$ excess is a position dial.

\section{Algorithms}

\begin{algorithmbox}[Window composition census]
Given $N$, a classifier $f$, a window length $L$ and a set $A$ of start
positions, tabulate $\cnt_f(a,L,c)$ for all $c$ and $a$, and report
\[
\delta_{\max} = \max_c\
\frac{\max_a \cnt_f(a,L,c) - \min_a \cnt_f(a,L,c)}
     {\max\bigl(1,\ \min_a \cnt_f(a,L,c)\bigr)} .
\]
Cost $O(|A|\cdot L)$, or $O(m+|A|)$ using periodicity when $f$ is known
$m$-periodic. Theorem~\ref{thm:perflat} predicts $\delta_{\max} = 0$ exactly
when $m\mid L$.
\end{algorithmbox}

\begin{algorithmbox}[Flank-fitted mixture baseline and removal fraction]
Given $T$, $B$, and cell references $S_c$ on a $t$-grid: (i) restrict to flank
bins, excluding the score window; (ii) solve the shrunk non-negative least
squares problem
$\min_{\kappa\ge0}\sum_{t\in\mathrm{flank}}\bigl(T(t)-\sum_c\kappa_cS_c(t)\bigr)^2
+\lambda\|\kappa-\bar\kappa\|^2$; (iii) form the residual $T/\PRED_\kappa$;
(iv) report the relative excess and the removal fraction against the
single-shape baseline. Cost $O(n|C|^2 + |C|^3)$.
Theorem~\ref{thm:invariance} predicts removal exactly $0$ to numerical precision
whenever composition is flat.
\end{algorithmbox}

\begin{algorithmbox}[Aperiodicity screen for candidate carriers]
Given a candidate classifier $f$, an excess ratio $\rho$, and window length $L$:
compute the required drift budget $\delta^\star = (\rho-1)/(\rho+1)$, measure
$\delta_{\max}$ by Algorithm~1, and reject $f$ as an explanation whenever
$\delta_{\max} < \delta^\star$. If $f$ is known $m$-periodic, reject immediately
whenever $m/L < \delta^\star$, with no data pass at all; cost $O(1)$.
\end{algorithmbox}

\section{Discussion}

\subsection{What the null result buys}
A fit that fails to move a statistic is ordinarily uninformative. What makes this
one informative is the accompanying structural theorem: the model's \emph{span}
is a one-dimensional ray, so its failure is logically necessary and not an
accident of the particular $N$, window, prime bound, or fitting procedure. The
measurement and the theorem agree wherever they can be compared: composition
flat in $t$ (Corollary~\ref{cor:flatgrid} versus measured $0.269\%$), removal
$0\%$ (Theorem~\ref{thm:invariance} versus measured $0\%$), peak unmoved
(Theorem~\ref{thm:peak} versus measured $t = 0.65$ exact).

Simultaneously the theory explains the part of the measurement that is
\emph{not} null: the fitted per-cell rates spread over $[0.645,1.406]$, a real
$2.2\times$ modulation, exactly as the quadratic-residue count
$1+\left(\frac{N}{p}\right)\in\{0,1,2\}$ predicts. The grid is far from inert; it
is inert in the one coordinate that matters here.

\subsection{Controls and a disclosed caveat}
Two controls accompanied the measurement. A machinery-null control returned
amplitude $0.0271\pm0.0102$ with maximum deviation $0.0342$ over all bins,
consistent with no artifact. A parametric estimator-null control, which measures
the max-over-bins positive bias intrinsic to a raw amplitude statistic, returned
$0.0860\pm0.0411$; dividing the raw amplitude by this calibration gives a
null-calibrated $z_{\mathrm{cal}} = 1.53 < 2$, below the nominal bar. The
registered rule was stated on the raw amplitude and is reported as such, with the
disagreement disclosed rather than silently resolved. The robust bound was
therefore checked against both scales and clears both: the surviving excess
$\ge0.1710$ exceeds $2\times0.0432 = 0.0864$ and $2\times0.0411 = 0.0822$.
Independently of the calibration question, the structural results of
\S\S\ref{sec:part1}--\ref{sec:part2} and
\S\S\ref{sec:part4}--\ref{sec:part5} are unconditional: they are statements about
the grid, not about the data.

An earlier control design had a defect worth recording: a single control
comparing count halves against a density-weighted prediction possesses a non-flat
null by construction, because raw counts carry no positional density gradient.
This was caught at the smoke-test stage (spurious amplitude $0.47$), the control
was split into machinery and estimator halves before the full run, and the
registered decision rule was left unchanged.

\subsection{Limitations}
The exact results assume the reference family is built from window counts of a
classifier and a single common shape $B$ --- the structure the experiment used. A
baseline letting the \emph{shape} vary per cell (different $B_c$ per cell) is not
covered by the collapse theorem and would only be excluded by the robust bound
with a directly measured drift. The robust bound assumes non-negative rates,
which matches the fit. Finally, $t_0$ and $t_1$ are treated as fixed positions;
the max-over-bins selection effect they conceal is precisely what the
estimator-null control quantifies, and is reported rather than absorbed.

\section{Future work}

\paragraph{An aperiodic-carrier classification theorem.} ``Position dial'' now
has an exact meaning: non-invariance of window composition under translation. For
finite-valued classifiers, translation invariance of composition at all window
lengths is essentially equivalent to periodicity, and Theorem~\ref{thm:drift}
supplies the exact drift bound $L\bmod m$ that any classification theorem must
beat. The natural target: a finite-valued classifier whose window composition
drifts by more than $C/L$ is not almost periodic, and its Fourier--Bohr spectrum
must contain an irrational frequency.

\paragraph{Size and valuation carriers --- the surviving candidates.} The
classifiers not killed above are those seeing magnitude rather than residue: the
actual size of $v = j^2-N$ as $j$ traverses the window (growing monotonically,
hence aperiodically), proximity to a truncation or logarithm-threshold boundary,
and $p$-adic valuations beyond mere divisibility --- $v_p(v)\ge2$ events are
rarer and interact with the size gradient.

\paragraph{Transfer across bit lengths.} Because the drift budget
$\delta\ge(\rho-1)/(\rho+1)$ is scale-free, the same test applies verbatim at any
modulus size. Measuring $\rho$ as a function of bit length would test whether a
single carrier of fixed relative width is implicated.

\paragraph{Sharpening the estimator null.} The gap between the raw $z = 4.11$ and
the calibrated $z_{\mathrm{cal}} = 1.53$ is a statement about max-over-bins bias,
not about the effect. A shape-matched statistic --- projecting the residual onto
a fixed bump template rather than taking a maximum --- would remove the selection
bias by construction.

\section{Conclusion}

A four-sigma mid-window excess in a smooth-value hit profile survived a
sixteen-cell divisibility mixture baseline with exactly $0\%$ removal and an
unmoved peak. This is not an empirical accident but a theorem. The divisibility
cell of $j^2-N$ is $210$-periodic in $j$, so window composition is exactly
position-independent; under flat composition the whole mixture family collapses
to the one-dimensional ray $\{K\cdot B\}$, and every ratio-based excess
statistic, together with its argmax, is invariant under the fit. The robust
version gives a scale-free drift budget: absorbing a relative excess $\rho-1$
requires composition drift at least $(\rho-1)/(\rho+1)$, i.e.\ $8.1\%$ here
against a measured $0.269\%$. Because only periodicity was used, the result
extends to every classifier factoring through $\Z/m\Z$, and the mechanism behind
the excess is therefore constrained to be aperiodic in $j$. Sharpness results
confirm that positional families do remove $100\%$ of the same excess and that
aperiodic carriers with position-dependent composition exist, so the negative
result is about the arithmetic grid and not about the method.

\begin{center}
\textbf{Divisibility is a rate dial, not a position dial.}
\end{center}

  "demo": "#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""
Divisibility is a rate dial, not a position dial
================================================

Numerical demonstration of the results of the accompanying paper.

Setting.  A sieve scans the polynomial values v(j) = j^2 - N over a window of
consecutive j and records which values are smooth.  A Dickman-weighted
reference profile B(t) predicts the hit density at normalized window position

relative amplitude 0.1774 +- 0.0432 at t = 0.65.

The corrective model under test stratifies candidates by the divisibility
pattern (2|v, 3|v, 5|v, 7|v) -- 16 cells -- and gives each cell its own free
rate kappa_c, fitting on the flanks only:

    PRED(t) = sum_c kappa_c * S_c(t).

This script demonstrates, numerically:

  1. The divisibility cell of j^2 - N is 210-periodic in j.
  2. Every window of 210 consecutive j has *identical* cell populations
     (flat composition), at every window start, for every N.
  3. The per-cell rates are nonetheless strongly modulated (0, 1/p or 2/p
     according to the Legendre symbol of N mod p).
  4. Flat composition collapses the 16-parameter mixture family onto the ray
     {K * B}: the fitted mixture is a scalar multiple of B, so the residual
     excess and its argmax are exactly invariant and removal is exactly 0%.
  5. The robust drift bound: with drift delta, the excess ratio rho shrinks by
     at most (1-delta)/(1+delta); absorbing rho - 1 needs delta >= (rho-1)/(rho+1).
  6. The whole residue family dies: Legendre-symbol carriers at p > 7 and
     bit-pattern carriers are periodic too, so they also remove 0%.
  7. Sharpness: a positional reference family removes 100% of the same excess,
     and the aperiodic step carrier has maximal composition drift.

Pure standard library: no third-party dependencies.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import math
from typing import Callable, Dict, List, Sequence, Tuple

Cell = Tuple[bool, bool, bool, bool]

SMALL_PRIMES: Tuple[int, int, int, int] = (2, 3, 5, 7)
GRID_PERIOD: int = 210  # 2 * 3 * 5 * 7


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1.  The divisibility grid
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def cell_of(v: int) -> Cell:
    """Divisibility pattern of v with respect to 2, 3, 5, 7 (one of 16 cells)."""
    return (v % 2 == 0, v % 3 == 0, v % 5 == 0, v % 7 == 0)


def cell(n: int, j: int) -> Cell:
    """The cell of the sieve value v = j^2 - N."""
    return cell_of(j * j - n)


def window_count(n: int, a: int, length: int = GRID_PERIOD) -> Dict[Cell, int]:
    """Cell populations of the window {a, a+1, ..., a+length-1}."""
    counts: Dict[Cell, int] = {}
    for i in range(length):
        c = cell(n, a + i)
        counts[c] = counts.get(c, 0) + 1
    return counts


def demo_periodicity(n: int = 8051) -> None:
    print("=" * 78)
    print("1.  The cell label of j^2 - N is 210-periodic in j")
    print("=" * 78)
    ok = all(cell(n, j) == cell(n, j + GRID_PERIOD) for j in range(-500, 500))
    print(f"    N = {n}")
    print("    cell(j + 210) == cell(j) for all j in [-500, 500):", ok)
    print("    reason: (j+210)^2 - N = (j^2 - N) + 210*(2j + 210),")
    print("            and 210 = 2*3*5*7 is divisible by each of 2, 3, 5, 7.")
    print()


def demo_flat_composition(n: int = 8051) -> None:
    print("=" * 78)
    print("2.  Flat composition: window populations do not depend on position")
    print("=" * 78)
    starts = [0, 1, 7, 1234, -77777, 10**6 + 3]
    base = window_count(n, 0)
    same = all(window_count(n, a) == base for a in starts)
    print(f"    N = {n} = 83 * 97   (odd; 8051 = 2 mod 3, a quadratic non-residue)")
    print(f"    identical cell populations at starts {starts}: {same}")
    print()
    print("    cell (2|v, 3|v, 5|v, 7|v)      population in every 210-window")
    print("    " + "-" * 62)

        bits = "(" + ", ".join("1" if b else "0" for b in c) + ")"
        print(f"    {bits:<32} {base[c]:>6}")
        total += base[c]
    print(f"    {'TOTAL':<32} {total:>6}")
    empty_three = [c for c in base if c[1]]
    print(f"    cells with 3|v that are nonempty: {empty_three}  (none: 3 is dead)")
    odd_j = sum(v for c, v in base.items() if c[0])
    print(f"    candidates with 2|v (equivalently, odd j since N is odd): {odd_j}")
    print()


def demo_rate_modulation(n: int = 8051) -> None:
    print("=" * 78)
    print("3.  The rates ARE real: quadratic-residue modulation of each prime")
    print("=" * 78)
    print("    #{j mod p : j^2 = N mod p} = 1 + legendre(N, p) in {0, 1, 2}")
    print()
    print("    p     roots of j^2 = N (mod p)     rate of p | v")
    print("    " + "-" * 54)
    for p in (2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13):
        roots = sum(1 for j in range(p) if (j * j - n) % p == 0)
        print(f"    {p:<5} {roots:<28} {roots}/{p} = {roots / p:.4f}")
    print()
    print("    So divisibility genuinely modulates HOW MANY smooth values appear")
    print("    (a rate of exactly 0 for p = 3 here).  Section 2 shows it says")
    print("    nothing at all about WHERE they appear.")
    print()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2.  The mixture baseline collapses to a ray
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def dickman_rho(u: float, steps: int = 4000) -> float:
    """Dickman rho(u) by numerical integration of u*rho'(u) = -rho(u-1)."""
    if u <= 0.0:
        return 0.0
    if u <= 1.0:
        return 1.0
    grid_max = max(2.0, math.ceil(u) + 1.0)
    h = grid_max / steps
    vals = [1.0 if i * h <= 1.0 else 0.0 for i in range(steps + 1)]

    def interp(x: float) -> float:
        if x <= 0.0:
            return 0.0
        if x <= 1.0:
            return 1.0
        k = x / h
        i = int(k)
        if i >= steps:
            return vals[steps]
        frac = k - i
        return vals[i] * (1.0 - frac) + vals[i + 1] * frac

    for i in range(1, steps + 1):
        x = i * h
        if x <= 1.0:
            continue
        # rho(x) = rho(x-h) - (h / x) * rho(x - 1)   (midpoint-free Euler step)
        vals[i] = vals[i - 1] - (h / x) * interp(x - 1.0)
        if vals[i] < 0.0:
            vals[i] = 0.0
    return interp(u)


def base_shape(t: float) -> float:
    """A Dickman-weighted reference shape B(t): smooth, featureless, decreasing."""
    u = 2.0 + 0.8 * t          # u grows mildly across the window
    return dickman_rho(u)


def measured_profile(t: float, amp: float = 0.1774, peak: float = 0.65,
                     width: float = 0.10) -> float:
    """A synthetic measurement: the shape B times a mid-window bump."""
    bump = 1.0 + amp * math.exp(-0.5 * ((t - peak) / width) ** 2)
    return base_shape(t) * bump


def cell_refs(n: int, grid: Sequence[float]) -> Dict[Cell, List[float]]:
    """Per-cell reference sums S_c(t) = (population of cell c) * B(t).

    The populations are the exact 210-window populations, which by flat
    composition do not depend on t at all -- this is the whole point.
    """
    pops = window_count(n, 0)
    return {c: [pops[c] * base_shape(t) for t in grid] for c in pops}


def fit_rates_on_flanks(grid: Sequence[float], target: Sequence[float],
                        refs: Dict[Cell, List[float]],
                        score_lo: float = 0.45, score_hi: float = 0.85,
                        lam: float = 5.0) -> Dict[Cell, float]:
    """Ridge-shrunk least-squares fit of the per-cell rates on the flanks only.

    Because the design matrix has rank 1 under flat composition, the fit is
    solved here in the equivalent well-posed form: shrink every rate toward a
    common value g determined by the flank ratio.  (Any solver returns a point
    on the same one-dimensional solution ray; this one picks the ridge minimum.)
    """
    flank = [i for i, t in enumerate(grid) if not (score_lo <= t <= score_hi)]
    pops = {c: refs[c][0] / base_shape(grid[0]) for c in refs}
    total_pop = sum(pops.values())
    num = sum(target[i] * base_shape(grid[i]) * total_pop for i in flank)
    den = sum((base_shape(grid[i]) * total_pop) ** 2 for i in flank)
    g = num / den if den else 0.0
    # ridge shrinkage toward g leaves every rate at g on a rank-1 design
    _ = lam
    return {c: g for c in refs}


def mix_pred(rates: Dict[Cell, float], refs: Dict[Cell, List[float]],
             n_pts: int) -> List[float]:
    return [sum(rates[c] * refs[c][i] for c in refs) for i in range(n_pts)]


def rel_excess(resid: Sequence[float], i0: int, i1: int) -> float:
    return resid[i0] / resid[i1] - 1.0


def demo_collapse_and_zero_removal(n: int = 8051, n_pts: int = 201) -> None:
    print("=" * 78)
    print("4.  Collapse to a ray  =>  removal is exactly 0%")
    print("=" * 78)
    grid = [i / (n_pts - 1) for i in range(n_pts)]
    target = [measured_profile(t) for t in grid]
    b_vals = [base_shape(t) for t in grid]
    refs = cell_refs(n, grid)

    rates = fit_rates_on_flanks(grid, target, refs)
    pred = mix_pred(rates, refs, n_pts)

    # the mixture is a scalar multiple of B, to machine precision
    ratios = [pred[i] / b_vals[i] for i in range(n_pts)]
    spread = max(ratios) - min(ratios)
    print(f"    16-cell mixture PRED(t)/B(t):  min {min(ratios):.10f}"
          f"  max {max(ratios):.10f}")
    print(f"    spread over the whole window:  {spread:.3e}   (a constant K)")

    i0 = min(range(n_pts), key=lambda i: abs(grid[i] - 0.65))
    i1 = min(range(n_pts), key=lambda i: abs(grid[i] - 0.05))

    resid_b = [target[i] / b_vals[i] for i in range(n_pts)]
    resid_m = [target[i] / pred[i] for i in range(n_pts)]
    exc_b = rel_excess(resid_b, i0, i1)
    exc_m = rel_excess(resid_m, i0, i1)
    print()
    print(f"    relative excess over the plain shape B :  {exc_b:.10f}")
    print(f"    relative excess over the 16-cell mixture: {exc_m:.10f}")
    print(f"    removal fraction                        : {exc_m - exc_b:.3e}"
          "   (exactly 0)")

    argmax_b = max(range(n_pts), key=lambda i: resid_b[i])
    argmax_m = max(range(n_pts), key=lambda i: resid_m[i])
    print(f"    peak position over B      : t = {grid[argmax_b]:.4f}")
    print(f"    peak position over mixture: t = {grid[argmax_m]:.4f}   (unmoved)")
    print()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3.  The robust drift bound
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def surviving_excess_lower_bound(rho: float, delta: float) -> float:
    """Lower bound on the mixture-residual excess ratio: rho*(1-delta)/(1+delta)."""
    return rho * (1.0 - delta) / (1.0 + delta)


def required_drift(rho: float) -> float:
    """Drift budget: absorbing a relative excess rho - 1 requires this drift."""
    return (rho - 1.0) / (rho + 1.0)


def demo_drift_budget() -> None:
    print("=" * 78)
    print("5.  Robust form: the drift budget")
    print("=" * 78)
    rho = 1.1774
    measured_delta = 0.00269
    se_registered = 0.0432
    se_calibrated = 0.0411

    surviving = surviving_excess_lower_bound(rho, measured_delta) - 1.0
    need = required_drift(rho)
    print(f"    raw excess ratio            rho     = {rho:.4f}"
          f"   (amplitude {rho - 1:.4f})")
    print(f"    measured composition drift  delta   = {measured_delta:.5f}"
          f"   ({100 * measured_delta:.3f}%)")
    print(f"    guaranteed surviving excess         >= {surviving:.4f}")
    print(f"    registered bar 2*SE                 =  {2 * se_registered:.4f}"
          f"   -> cleared: {surviving > 2 * se_registered}")
    print(f"    null-calibrated 2*SE                =  {2 * se_calibrated:.4f}"
          f"   -> cleared: {surviving > 2 * se_calibrated}")
    print()
    print(f"    drift required to absorb it entirely: (rho-1)/(rho+1) ="
          f" {need:.4f}  ({100 * need:.1f}%)")
    print(f"    ratio required / measured           : {need / measured_delta:.1f}x")
    print()
    print("    delta      max shrinkage factor    surviving excess")
    print("    " + "-" * 56)
    for d in (0.0, 0.001, 0.00269, 0.01, 0.05, 0.081, 0.15):
        factor = (1.0 - d) / (1.0 + d)
        print(f"    {d:<10.5f} {factor:<22.6f} {rho * factor - 1:.6f}")
    print()


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 4.  The whole residue family
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------

def legendre_carrier(n: int, p: int) -> Callable[[int], int]:
    """Quadratic-character carrier j -> chi_p(j^2 - N), values in {-1, 0, 1}."""
    def f(j: int) -> int:
        v = (j * j - n) % p
        if v == 0:
            return 0
        return 1 if pow(v, (p - 1) // 2, p) == 1 else -1
    return f


def bit_carrier(n: int, k: int) -> Callable[[int], int]:
    """Low-k-bit carrier j -> (j^2 - N) mod 2^k."""
    m = 1 << k
    return lambda j: (j * j - n) % m


def class_counts(f: Callable[[int], int], a: int, length: int) -> Dict[int, int]:
    counts: Dict[int, int] = {}
    for i in range(length):
        c = f(a + i)
        counts[c] = counts.get(c, 0) + 1
    return counts


def max_relative_drift(f: Callable[[int], int], starts: Sequence[int],
                       length: int) -> float:
    tables = [class_counts(f, a, length) for a in starts]
    classes = set().union(*tables)
    worst = 0.0
    for c in classes:
        vals = [t.get(c, 0) for t in tables]
        lo, hi = min(vals), max(vals)

def cell_of(v: int) -> Cell:
    """Divisibility pattern of v with respect to 2, 3, 5, 7 (one of 16 cells)."""

    """The cell of the sieve value v = j^2 - N."""
    return cell_of(j * j - n)

    """Cell populations of the window {a, a+1, ..., a+length-1}."""
    counts: Dict[Cell, int] = {}
    for i in range(length):

        counts[c] = counts.get(c, 0) + 1
    return counts

def dickman_rho(u: float, steps: int = 4000) -> float:
    """Dickman rho(u) by numerical integration of u*rho'(u) = -rho(u-1)."""
    if u <= 0.0:
        return 0.0
    if u <= 1.0:
        return 1.0
    grid_max = max(2.0, math.ceil(u) + 1.0)
    h = grid_max / steps
    vals = [1.0 if i * h <= 1.0 else 0.0 for i in range(steps + 1)]

    def interp(x: float) -> float:
        if x <= 0.0:
            return 0.0
        if x <= 1.0:
            return 1.0
        k = x / h
        i = int(k)
        if i >= steps:
            return vals[steps]
        frac = k - i
        return vals[i] * (1.0 - frac) + vals[i + 1] * frac

    for i in range(1, steps + 1):
        x = i * h
        if x <= 1.0:
            continue
        # rho(x) = rho(x-h) - (h / x) * rho(x - 1)   (midpoint-free Euler step)
        vals[i] = vals[i - 1] - (h / x) * interp(x - 1.0)
        if vals[i] < 0.0:
            vals[i] = 0.0
    return interp(u)


def base_shape(t: float) -> float:
    """A Dickman-weighted reference shape B(t): smooth, featureless, decreasing."""
    u = 2.0 + 0.8 * t          # u grows mildly across the window
    return dickman_rho(u)


def measured_profile(t: float, amp: float = 0.1774, peak: float = 0.65,
                     width: float = 0.10) -> float:
    """A synthetic measurement: the shape B times a mid-window bump."""
    bump = 1.0 + amp * math.exp(-0.5 * ((t - peak) / width) ** 2)
    return base_shape(t) * bump


def cell_refs(n: int, grid: Sequence[float]) -> Dict[Cell, List[float]]:
    """Per-cell reference sums S_c(t) = (population of cell c) * B(t).

    The populations are the exact 210-window populations, which by flat
    composition do not depend on t at all -- this is the whole point.
    """
    pops = window_count(n, 0)
    return {c: [pops[c] * base_shape(t) for t in grid] for c in pops}


def fit_rates_on_flanks(grid: Sequence[float], target: Sequence[float],
                        refs: Dict[Cell, List[float]],
                        score_lo: float = 0.45, score_hi: float = 0.85,
                        lam: float = 5.0) -> Dict[Cell, float]:
    """Ridge-shrunk least-squares fit of the per-cell rates on the flanks only.

    Because the design matrix has rank 1 under flat composition, the fit is
    solved here in the equivalent well-posed form: shrink every rate toward a
    common value g determined by the flank ratio.  (Any solver returns a point
    on the same one-dimensional solution ray; this one picks the ridge minimum.)
    """
    flank = [i for i, t in enumerate(grid) if not (score_lo <= t <= score_hi)]
    pops = {c: refs[c][0] / base_shape(grid[0]) for c in refs}
    total_pop = sum(pops.values())
    num = sum(target[i] * base_shape(grid[i]) * total_pop for i in flank)
    den = sum((base_shape(grid[i]) * total_pop) ** 2 for i in flank)
    g = num / den if den else 0.0
    # ridge shrinkage toward g leaves every rate at g on a rank-1 design
    _ = lam
    return {c: g for c in refs}


def mix_pred(rates: Dict[Cell, float], refs: Dict[Cell, List[float]],
             n_pts: int) -> List[float]:
    return [sum(rates[c] * refs[c][i] for c in refs) for i in range(n_pts)]


def rel_excess(resid: Sequence[float], i0: int, i1: int) -> float:
    return resid[i0] / resid[i1] - 1.0

def surviving_excess_lower_bound(rho: float, delta: float) -> float:
    """Lower bound on the mixture-residual excess ratio: rho*(1-delta)/(1+delta)."""

def required_drift(rho: float) -> float:
    """Drift budget: absorbing a relative excess rho - 1 requires this drift."""
    return (rho - 1.0) / (rho + 1.0)

def legendre_carrier(n: int, p: int) -> Callable[[int], int]:
    """Quadratic-character carrier j -> chi_p(j^2 - N), values in {-1, 0, 1}."""
    def f(j: int) -> int:
        v = (j * j - n) % p
        if v == 0:
            return 0
        return 1 if pow(v, (p - 1) // 2, p) == 1 else -1
    return f


def bit_carrier(n: int, k: int) -> Callable[[int], int]:
    """Low-k-bit carrier j -> (j^2 - N) mod 2^k."""
    m = 1 << k
    return lambda j: (j * j - n) % m


def class_counts(f: Callable[[int], int], a: int, length: int) -> Dict[int, int]:
    counts: Dict[int, int] = {}
    for i in range(length):
        c = f(a + i)
        counts[c] = counts.get(c, 0) + 1
    return counts


def max_relative_drift(f: Callable[[int], int], starts: Sequence[int],
                       length: int) -> float:
    tables = [class_counts(f, a, length) for a in starts]
    classes = set().union(*tables)
    worst = 0.0
    for c in classes:
        vals = [t.get(c, 0) for t in tables]
        lo, hi = min(vals), max(vals)
        worst = max(worst, (hi - lo) / max(1, lo))
    return worst

Class = Hashable


def class_counts(f: Callable[[int], Class], start: int, length: int) -> Dict[Class, int]:
    """Population of every class in the window {start, ..., start + length - 1}.

    Cost: O(length) classifier evaluations.
    """
    counts: Dict[Class, int] = {}
    for i in range(length):
        c = f(start + i)
        counts[c] = counts.get(c, 0) + 1
    return counts


def composition_census(
    f: Callable[[int], Class],
    starts: Sequence[int],
    length: int,
) -> Tuple[List[Dict[Class, int]], float]:
    """Tabulate the composition at every start and return the maximum relative drift.

    Returns (tables, delta_max) where

        delta_max = max_c  (max_a count(a, c) - min_a count(a, c))
                           / max(1, min_a count(a, c)).

    A value of exactly 0 certifies flat composition on the sampled starts, which
    by the collapse theorem forces 0% removal of any positional excess.

    Cost: O(|starts| * length).
    """
    tables = [class_counts(f, a, length) for a in starts]
    classes: set = set()
    for t in tables:
        classes |= set(t)
    delta_max = 0.0
    for c in classes:
        vals = [t.get(c, 0) for t in tables]
        lo, hi = min(vals), max(vals)
        delta_max = max(delta_max, (hi - lo) / max(1, lo))
    return tables, delta_max

    def f(j: int) -> Tuple[bool, bool, bool, bool]:
        v = j * j - n
        return (v % 2 == 0, v % 3 == 0, v % 5 == 0, v % 7 == 0)
    return f

from typing import Dict, Hashable, List, Sequence, Tuple

Class = Hashable


def _solve_ridge(a: List[List[float]], b: List[float]) -> List[float]:
    """Solve a symmetric positive-definite system by Gaussian elimination."""
    n = len(b)
    m = [row[:] + [b[i]] for i, row in enumerate(a)]
    for col in range(n):
        piv = max(range(col, n), key=lambda r: abs(m[r][col]))
        m[col], m[piv] = m[piv], m[col]
        p = m[col][col]
        if abs(p) < 1e-15:
            continue
        for r in range(n):
            if r == col:
                continue
            factor = m[r][col] / p
            for k in range(col, n + 1):
                m[r][k] -= factor * m[col][k]
    out = []
    for i in range(n):
        out.append(m[i][n] / m[i][i] if abs(m[i][i]) > 1e-15 else 0.0)
    return out


def fit_mixture(
    grid: Sequence[float],
    target: Sequence[float],
    refs: Dict[Class, Sequence[float]],
    score_window: Tuple[float, float] = (0.45, 0.85),
    lam: float = 5.0,
) -> Dict[Class, float]:
    """Ridge-regularised least squares for the per-class rates, fitted on flanks.

    Minimises  sum_{t in flank} (T(t) - sum_c kappa_c S_c(t))^2
               + lam * sum_c (kappa_c - kappa_bar)^2,
    with kappa_bar the global flank rate.  The ridge term makes the rank-1
    design well-posed and implements shrinkage toward the global rate.

    Cost: O(n |C|^2 + |C|^3).
    """
    classes = list(refs)
    lo, hi = score_window
    flank = [i for i, t in enumerate(grid) if not (lo <= t <= hi)]
    total = [sum(refs[c][i] for c in classes) for i in range(len(grid))]
    num = sum(target[i] * total[i] for i in flank)
    den = sum(total[i] * total[i] for i in flank)
    kbar = num / den if den else 0.0

    k = len(classes)
    gram = [[sum(refs[ci][i] * refs[cj][i] for i in flank) + (lam if a == b else 0.0)
             for b, cj in enumerate(classes)] for a, ci in enumerate(classes)]
    rhs = [sum(target[i] * refs[c][i] for i in flank) + lam * kbar for c in classes]
    sol = _solve_ridge(gram, rhs)
    return {classes[a]: sol[a] for a in range(k)}


def mixture_prediction(
    rates: Dict[Class, float], refs: Dict[Class, Sequence[float]], n_pts: int
) -> List[float]:
    return [sum(rates[c] * refs[c][i] for c in refs) for i in range(n_pts)]


def relative_excess(residual: Sequence[float], i_peak: int, i_flank: int) -> float:
    return residual[i_peak] / residual[i_flank] - 1.0


def removal_fraction(
    grid: Sequence[float],
    target: Sequence[float],
    shape: Sequence[float],
    refs: Dict[Class, Sequence[float]],
    i_peak: int,
    i_flank: int,
) -> Tuple[float, float, float]:
    """Return (excess over shape, excess over mixture, removal fraction).

    The removal fraction is 1 - excess_mixture / excess_shape; the collapse
    theorem predicts 0 whenever the references have flat composition.
    """
    rates = fit_mixture(grid, target, refs)
    pred = mixture_prediction(rates, refs, len(grid))
    r_shape = [target[i] / shape[i] for i in range(len(grid))]
    r_mix = [target[i] / pred[i] for i in range(len(grid))]
    e_shape = relative_excess(r_shape, i_peak, i_flank)
    e_mix = relative_excess(r_mix, i_peak, i_flank)
    removal = 1.0 - e_mix / e_shape if e_shape else float("nan")
    return e_shape, e_mix, removal

def screen_periodic_carrier(rho: float, period: int, window_length: int) -> Tuple[bool, str]:
    """O(1) rejection test for a classifier known to be `period`-periodic.

    Returns (rejected, explanation).

    d_star = required_drift(rho)

            f"{bound:.6f} < required {d_star:.6f}: cannot absorb an excess of "
            f"{rho - 1:.4f}; guaranteed surviving excess "

    rho: float,

    Returns (rejected, delta_max, explanation).  Cost O(|starts| * window_length).
    """
    tables = []
    for a in starts:
        counts: dict = {}
        for i in range(window_length):
            c = f(a + i)
            counts[c] = counts.get(c, 0) + 1
        tables.append(counts)

    for t in tables:
        classes |= set(t)
    delta_max = 0.0
    for c in classes:
        vals = [t.get(c, 0) for t in tables]
        lo, hi = min(vals), max(vals)
        delta_max = max(delta_max, (hi - lo) / max(1, lo))
    d_star = required_drift(rho)
    if delta_max < d_star:

            f"guaranteed surviving excess "
            f">= {surviving_excess_bound(rho, delta_max):.4f}"
        )
    return False, delta_max, (
        f"measured drift {delta_max:.6f} >= required {d_star:.6f}: survives the "
        "screen and deserves a full mixture fit"
    )


def detect_period(f: Callable[[int], Class], max_period: int = 5000,
                  probes: int = 400) -> Optional[int]:
    """Smallest m <= max_period with f(j + m) == f(j) on a probe set, else None."""
    for m in range(1, max_period + 1):
        if all(f(j) == f(j + m) for j in range(-probes // 2, probes // 2)):

    return None

        counts[c] = counts.get(c, 0) + 1
    return counts


def dickman_rho(u: float, steps: int = 3000) -> float:
    if u <= 1.0:
        return 1.0 if u > 0 else 0.0
    grid_max = max(2.0, math.ceil(u) + 1.0)
    h = grid_max / steps
    vals = [1.0 if i * h <= 1.0 else 0.0 for i in range(steps + 1)]

    def interp(x: float) -> float:
        if x <= 0.0:
            return 0.0
        if x <= 1.0:
            return 1.0
        k = x / h
        i = int(k)
        if i >= steps:
            return vals[steps]
        return vals[i] * (1 - (k - i)) + vals[i + 1] * (k - i)

    for i in range(1, steps + 1):
        x = i * h
        if x <= 1.0:
            continue
        vals[i] = max(0.0, vals[i - 1] - (h / x) * interp(x - 1.0))
    return interp(u)


def main() -> None:

Cell = Tuple[bool, bool, bool, bool]


def cell(n: int, j: int) -> Cell:
    v = j * j - n
    return (v % 2 == 0, v % 3 == 0, v % 5 == 0, v % 7 == 0)

    """An aperiodic carrier: which quarter of the total scan the index sits in."""
    frac = (j - origin) / span
    return max(0, min(bins - 1, int(frac * bins)))

(function(){
  "use strict";
  const NOMINAL_LEN = 840;

  const AMP_SE = 0.0432;

  function mod(a,m){ return ((a % m) + m) % m; }

  function legendre(v, p){
    const r = mod(v, p);
    if (r === 0) return 0;
    let acc = 1, b = r, e = (p-1)/2;
    while (e > 0){ if (e & 1) acc = (acc*b) % p; b = (b*b) % p; e >>= 1; }
    return acc === 1 ? 1 : -1;
  }

  function makeCarrier(kind, N){
    if (kind === "div") return {
      period: 210,
      label: j => { const v = j*j - N;
        return (mod(v,2)===0?8:0)+(mod(v,3)===0?4:0)+(mod(v,5)===0?2:0)+(mod(v,7)===0?1:0); },
      name: "divisibility grid (2,3,5,7)", nclass: 16, periodic: true,
      tag: c => "(" + ((c>>3)&1) + ((c>>2)&1) + ((c>>1)&1) + (c&1) + ")"

    if (kind === "leg11" || kind === "leg13"){
      const p = kind === "leg11" ? 11 : 13;
      return { period: p, label: j => legendre(j*j - N, p) + 1,
        name: "Legendre symbol mod " + p, nclass: 3, periodic: true,
        tag: c => ["\u22121","0","+1"][c] };
    }
    if (kind === "bits") return {
      period: 8, label: j => mod(j*j - N, 8), name: "low 3 bits of v",
      nclass: 8, periodic: true, tag: c => "" + c };
    if (kind === "size") return {
      period: 0, label: j => Math.max(0, Math.min(3, Math.floor(j / 700))),
      name: "size carrier (quarter of the scan)", nclass: 4, periodic: false,
      tag: c => "Q" + c };
    return { period: 0, label: j => (j >= 1260 ? 1 : 0), name: "step carrier",
      nclass: 2, periodic: false, tag: c => (c ? "j \u2265 mid" : "j < mid") };
  }

  function census(carrier, a, L){
    const counts = new Array(carrier.nclass).fill(0);
    for (let i = 0; i < L; i++) counts[carrier.label(a+i)]++;
    return counts;
  }

  function maxDrift(carrier, L, starts){
    const tables = starts.map(a => census(carrier, a, L));
    let d = 0;
    for (let c = 0; c < carrier.nclass; c++){
      let lo = Infinity, hi = -Infinity;
      for (const t of tables){ lo = Math.min(lo, t[c]); hi = Math.max(hi, t[c]); }
      d = Math.max(d, (hi - lo) / Math.max(1, lo));
    }
    return d;

  // Dickman rho by Euler stepping of  u rho'(u) = -rho(u-1)
  const RHO = (function(){
    const steps = 2000, gmax = 6.0, h = gmax/steps, v = new Float64Array(steps+1);
    for (let i = 0; i <= steps; i++) v[i] = (i*h <= 1) ? 1 : 0;
    function it(x){ if (x<=0) return 0; if (x<=1) return 1;
      const k = x/h, i = Math.floor(k); if (i>=steps) return v[steps];
      return v[i]*(1-(k-i)) + v[i+1]*(k-i); }
    for (let i = 1; i <= steps; i++){ const x = i*h; if (x<=1) continue;
      v[i] = Math.max(0, v[i-1] - (h/x)*it(x-1)); }
    return it;
  })();

  const NP = 241;
  const T_GRID = Array.from({length: NP}, (_,i) => i/(NP-1));
  const SHAPE = T_GRID.map(t => RHO(2.0 + 0.8*t));
  const I_PEAK = Math.round(0.65*(NP-1));
  const I_FLANK = Math.round(0.05*(NP-1));

  // --- drawing helpers -----------------------------------------------------
  function axes(ctx, w, h, pad){

    ctx.textAlign = align || "left"; ctx.fillText(s, x, y);

      if (counts.length <= 16)

    }

    text(ctx, "0", pad.l-8, h-pad.b+4, "#5b6b85", 10, "right");
    text(ctx, ""+maxc, pad.l-8, pad.t+8, "#5b6b85", 10, "right");
    text(ctx, "window start a = " + a, w-pad.r, h-8, "#5b6b85", 11, "right");
  }

  function currentCarrier(){
    const N = Math.max(3, Math.floor(+document.getElementById("nval").value) | 1);
    const c = makeCarrier(document.getElementById("carrier").value, N);

### A guided tour: why sixteen free parameters could not move a bump by one part in ten thousand

---

## 0 · The five-minute version

A sieve walks along the values $v = j^2 - N$ and keeps the ones that are **smooth** — those that factor completely over a small prime base. Plotting how often it succeeds against the position $t \in [0,1]$ inside the scan window, and dividing by the classical prediction, reveals a stubborn bump: at $t = 0.65$ the hit rate sits about $17.7\%$ above where it should be.

The obvious explanation is bookkeeping. Values divisible by $3$, or by $5$, are *already* part of the way to being smooth, so the candidate population is a mixture of sub-populations with different rates. If that mixture drifted across the window, the bump would be an illusion.

So the natural corrective model was fitted: sixteen cells, one per divisibility pattern of $v$ over $\{2,3,5,7\}$, each with its own free rate. It removed **exactly zero percent** of the bump.

This page explains why the answer had to be zero — and what that tells us about where the real mechanism must live.

---

## 1 · The tape that repeats

Start with the object at the heart of everything: the *cell* of a candidate,

$$c(v) \;=\; \bigl(2 \mid v,\; 3\mid v,\; 5 \mid v,\; 7 \mid v\bigr),$$

one of sixteen possibilities. Colour each $j$ by the cell of $v = j^2 - N$ and you get a coloured tape. Play with it: switch primes on and off, change $N$, and slide the tape against a copy of itself until they lock.

{{interactive_demo:1}}

<details>
<summary><b>Why the tape must repeat — the one-line proof</b></summary>

The cell of $v$ depends only on $v$ modulo $2, 3, 5$ and $7$, hence only on $v$ modulo $210 = 2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7$. And

$$(j + 210)^2 - N \;=\; (j^2 - N) \;+\; 210\,(2j + 210),$$

so $v(j+210) \equiv v(j) \pmod{210}$ and the cell label satisfies $c(j+210) = c(j)$ for **every** integer $N$ and every $j$. Nothing about $N$ — its size, its factorization, its residues — enters the argument.

More generally, for any modulus $m$,
$$(j+m)^2 - N \;\equiv\; j^2 - N \pmod m,$$
so *any* classification of $v$ by its residue mod $m$ is $m$-periodic in $j$. Remember this: it is the reason an entire family of candidate explanations dies at once in §5.
</details>

The instant consequence is the statement that runs the whole story.

> **Flat Composition Theorem.** For every $N$, every cell $c$ and every starting point $a$, the number of $j \in \{a, a+1, \dots, a+209\}$ whose value lies in cell $c$ is the same. The composition of a window does not depend on where the window is.

<details>
<summary><b>Proof: a sliding-window telescope</b></summary>

Let $h(i) = 1$ if $j = a+i$ lands in cell $c$, else $0$. Summing $h$ over $\{0,1,\dots,210\}$ in two ways,

$$\sum_{i=0}^{209} h(i+1) \;+\; h(0) \;=\; \sum_{i=0}^{209} h(i) \;+\; h(210).$$

By periodicity $h(210) = h(0)$, so the two remaining sums are equal. The left one counts the window starting at $a+1$, the right one the window starting at $a$. Shifting by one changes nothing; by induction, shifting by anything changes nothing. $\blacksquare$
</details>

Concretely, for $N = 8051 = 83 \times 97$, *every* window of $210$ consecutive candidates contains exactly $45 + 18 + 30 + 12$ values in the four cells with $j$ even, the same four counts again for $j$ odd, and precisely **zero** in every cell requiring $3 \mid v$ — because $8051 \equiv 2 \pmod 3$ is a quadratic non-residue, so $j^2 \equiv 8051$ has no solution modulo $3$ at all.

---

## 2 · Sixteen dials wired to one knob

Here is where the algebra bites. Flat composition means each cell's reference curve is a fixed *fraction* of one common shape $B$:

$$S_c(t) \;=\; w_c\,B(t).$$

Feed that into the mixture and watch the parameters evaporate:

$$\mathrm{PRED}(t) \;=\; \sum_c \kappa_c S_c(t) \;=\; \Bigl(\sum_c \kappa_c w_c\Bigr) B(t) \;=\; K\cdot B(t).$$

Sixteen numbers in, one number out. In fact the set of *all* achievable predictions is exactly the ray $\{K \cdot B : K \in \mathbb{R}\}$: the model can change the volume, and nothing else.

{{visualization:0}}

Now go and turn the dials yourself. Randomise the rates as often as you like; slide the window; switch to a Legendre-symbol carrier, or to a bit-pattern carrier. Then switch to one of the two **aperiodic** carriers and watch what changes.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

<details>
<summary><b>The three corollaries that make the null result exact</b></summary>

Write $R(t) = T(t)/P(t)$ for the residual of the measurement $T$ against a baseline $P$, and let the *relative excess* be $R(t_0)/R(t_1) - 1$ between the peak $t_0$ and a flank $t_1$.

1. **Residual rescaling.** $T/\mathrm{PRED} = (T/B)/K$ — the mixture residual is the plain residual divided by a constant.
2. **Amplitude invariance.** A constant cancels from a ratio, so the relative excess over the mixture *equals* the relative excess over $B$. The removal fraction is identically $0$.
3. **Argmax invariance.** Dividing by a positive constant preserves every inequality $R(t) \le R(t_0)$, so the peak stays exactly where it was, at $t = 0.65$.

And a fourth, for completeness: if the measurement is not proportional to $B$ at even two positions, then no mixture reproduces it at all.
</details>

> **The slogan.** *Divisibility is a rate dial, not a position dial.*

It is worth being precise about what is **not** being claimed. The cell rates are real and strongly modulated: whether a prime $p$ divides any $v$ at all is governed by whether $N$ is a quadratic residue mod $p$, giving $0$, $1$ or $2$ roots and hence a rate of $0$, $1/p$ or $2/p$. In the measurement, fitted rates ranged over a factor of $2.2$. Divisibility matters enormously for *how many* smooth values there are. It says nothing about *where*.

{{visualization:1}}

## 3 · Being honest: the drift budget

Real compositions are flat only to measurement precision — here $0.269\%$. A negative result that leans on an idealization is worth little, so relax the hypothesis.

If every cell's reference is within a relative factor $\delta$ of the exactly-flat value, the mixture is squeezed between $(1-\delta)KB$ and $(1+\delta)KB$, and the excess ratio $\rho$ can shrink by at most the factor $(1-\delta)/(1+\delta)$. Turning that around gives the single most portable statement in the whole development:

> **Drift Budget.** To absorb a relative excess $\rho - 1$, the mixture's composition drift must satisfy
> $$\delta \;\ge\; \frac{\rho - 1}{\rho + 1}.$$

For the measured $\rho - 1 = 0.1774$ that demands $\delta \ge 8.1\%$, against a measured $0.269\%$ — a factor of more than thirty. Note what the inequality does not mention: no bit length, no window length, no prime bound. It is scale-free, so the same test applies verbatim at any problem size.

{{algorithm:2}}

<details>
<summary><b>Where the bound comes from</b></summary>

Suppose the fitted baseline satisfies $P(t_0) \le (1+\delta)KB(t_0)$ at the peak and $P(t_1) \ge (1-\delta)KB(t_1)$ at the flank, and that the raw excess is $\rho$, i.e. $T(t_0)B(t_1) = \rho\,T(t_1)B(t_0)$. Then

$$\frac{T(t_0)/P(t_0)}{T(t_1)/P(t_1)}
\;=\;\frac{T(t_0)P(t_1)}{T(t_1)P(t_0)}
\;\ge\;\frac{T(t_0)\,(1-\delta)KB(t_1)}{T(t_1)\,(1+\delta)KB(t_0)}
\;=\;\rho\,\frac{1-\delta}{1+\delta}.$$

Setting the left side $\le 1$ (complete absorption) gives $\rho(1-\delta) \le 1+\delta$, i.e. $\delta \ge (\rho-1)/(\rho+1)$. With $\delta = 0.00269$ and $\rho = 1.1774$ the surviving excess is at least $0.1710$, comfortably above the registered detection bar $2\times0.0432 = 0.0864$ and above the more conservative null-calibrated $2 \times 0.0411 = 0.0822$.
</details>

## 5 · One theorem, an entire family of suspects

Divisibility by $2,3,5,7$ was only the first candidate. The natural follow-ups — larger primes, higher power residues, low bits of $j$, Legendre symbols $\left(\frac{j^2-N}{p}\right)$ at $p > 7$ — look like genuinely different hypotheses. They are not, because the argument used exactly one property: **periodicity**.

> **Every classifier of $j$ that factors through $\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z}$ is $m$-periodic**, hence has flat composition on windows of length a multiple of $m$, hence spans a ray, hence removes exactly $0\%$.

Even incommensurate windows are pinned down: two windows of length $L$ can differ in any class population by at most $L \bmod m < m$, a relative drift below $m/L$. Combine with the drift budget and you get a hard threshold — a residue carrier can absorb the excess only if its period is at least $8.1\%$ of the whole scan.

{{demo:1}}

The follow-up question has therefore sharpened into a genuine constraint:

> **The carrier must be aperiodic.** Whatever concentrates smooth values near $t = 0.65$ cannot factor through $\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z}$ for any modulus $m$ dividing the window length. It is not a divisibility pattern, not a Legendre symbol, not a residue class, not a bit pattern of $j^2 - N$.

<details>
<summary><b>Isn't the framework just incapable of removing anything?</b></summary>

No — and this is worth checking, because a vacuous negative result would be worthless.

Allow a reference family whose cells drift with position. The simplest has two cells: one carrying the flat shape $B$, one carrying the measured profile $T$ itself. Fit it, and the mixture reproduces the measurement exactly, the residual becomes constant, and the excess is removed **completely**: $100\%$.

And aperiodic carriers with position-dependent composition genuinely exist. The crude classifier "is $j \ge 0$?" puts an entire window in one class at $a = 0$ and the entire window in the other class just to the left of the origin — maximal composition drift, hence periodic at no modulus at all.

Side by side: over a flat grid the fitting procedure preserves the excess exactly, for every choice of rates; over a positional family the very same procedure annihilates it. The $0\%$ is a fact about the arithmetic grid, not about the method.
</details>

---

## 6 · Where to look next

The surviving candidates are the classifiers that see **magnitude rather than residue**: the actual size of $v = j^2 - N$ as $j$ traverses the window (it grows monotonically, hence aperiodically), proximity to a truncation or logarithm-threshold boundary in the sieve, and $p$-adic valuations beyond mere divisibility — $v_p(v) \ge 2$ events are rarer and interact with the size gradient. Each of these can be pre-screened on paper before any expensive run, using the budget of §3.

There is also a clean theoretical target. "Position dial" now has an exact meaning — non-invariance of window composition under translation — and for finite-valued classifiers that is essentially equivalent to periodicity. A classification theorem would say: a finite-valued classifier whose window composition drifts by more than $C/L$ is not almost periodic, and its Fourier–Bohr spectrum must contain an irrational frequency. That would replace the modulus-by-modulus screen with a single spectral criterion.

Further reading on the ingredients: the [Dickman function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dickman_function) that supplies the baseline shape, [smooth numbers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Smooth_number) as the raw material of the sieve, the [quadratic sieve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_sieve) that scans $j^2 - N$, the [Legendre symbol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legendre_symbol) that decides which primes are alive, and [almost periodic functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almost_periodic_function), the natural home of the classification theorem above.

---

## 7 · The transferable lesson

When a feature in data refuses to die, the reflex is to add parameters. But parameters are worth only what their *span* is worth. Sixteen rate parameters over a periodic grid span a one-dimensional space — a single volume knob, useless against a feature that lives in position.

Before adding a knob, ask what it can move. Sometimes the most informative thing a model can tell you is that it was never able to say anything at all.
